newsitem.title: USA: Mexico cenbank can control wobbly peso - US experts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico cenbank can control wobbly peso - US experts.

text.p: The Mexican peso has slipped in recent days, but the currency should continue its course of real appreciation as Mexico's central bank guides monetary policy, Wall Street economists said on Tuesday.
Market jitters weighing on the Mexican unit began Monday after news of changes in Mexico's petrochemical privatization.

But analysts at three major U.S. investment banks said the Mexican currency, the focus of market angst since its surprise devaluation of December 1994, would likely end the year around 7.9 pesos to the dollar, from Tuesday's level of 7.7 pesos.

Their confidence was inspired by the Mexican central bank, which has adopted the tactics of most industrialized nations by lifting its Cetes interest rate to control excessive market volatility, analysts said.

"As we have seen over the past two days, the monetary authorities will lead the market to higher rates that will be required to compensate for the recent peso weakness or for political uncertainty going forward," said Jose Barrionuevo, senior economist for Latin America at Chase Securities.
The peso has traditionally weakened into the end of a calendar year. But analysts said Mexico's economy is much stronger than it has been in past years.

U.S. economists pointed to Mexico's $601 international trade surplus in September as evidence that the peso's real appreciation had not affected the export sector, and said the trend of appreciation would likely persist.
"The forces toward the continued real appreciation of the peso are there - namely trade and capital flows," said Karim Abdel-Motaal, JP Morgan emerging markets research economist.
Two weeks ago, U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch, who correctly forecast the 1994 devaluation, warned that Mexico was allowing the peso to become overvalued again.

But JP Morgan's Abdel-Motaal said the Mexican currency remains around 20-30 percent undervalued on a wage cost basis and 10 percent undervalued on producer price basis, "If the peso were appreciating too much the most compelling evidence would be the trade accounts."
Barrionuevo noted that "it's very difficult to argue that the peso is overvalued when you see the kind of trade performance that we have seen this year."
He added that the country's 1996 trade levels had kept up with last year's performance as the economy had recovered.
But the peso's recent strength might complicate the country's ability to post strong exports next year, said Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist at ING Barings.

"We wouldn't want the peso to go from 7.75 toward 8.0 overnight, but it is high time for the peso to be nudged towards 8.0 in the next three months or so, for the Bank of Mexico to declare victory over inflation, and ease up on its highly restrictive monetary policy," Porzecanski said.
U.S. analysts thoroughly rejected market speculation that the Bank of Mexico had tinkered with the exchange rate to produce this year's performance.

"They are doing exactly what they should be doing to meet their secondary objective, namely to prevent a huge slide in the peso in one way or the other," Abdel-Motaal said. "The result of that has been a slight rise in interest rates."
